clue.text: The Spanish miss having enough characters to fill all this!

definitions.meaning: the Spanish word for an unmarried young woman, used like Miss

definitions.text: having enough characters to fill all this!
definitions.meaning: every other answer in the grid is spelt only from the eight letters of this word

explanation.surface: A young Spanish woman with a name long enough to fill the whole grid.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition describes the theme: every answer in the puzzle uses only the letters S, E, N, O, R, I, T and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Señorita is the Spanish title for an unmarried woman, the equivalent of Miss.

clue.text: Wind-up twizzle-stick

definitions.meaning: someone who deliberately provokes or teases others, a troublemaker
a little stick for mixing a drink

explanation.definitionFit: A troublemaker stirs things up among people; a cocktail stick physically stirs a drink.

clue.text: Staffroom paper undelivered? Letters quickly written

parts.note: if the paper has not been delivered there is no paper
the TES (Times Educational Supplement) is the weekly paper read by British teachers

explanation.surface: A teacher complains the staffroom newspaper never arrived, while dashing off quick messages.
explanation.walkthrough: The TES is the Times Educational Supplement, Britain's teachers' newspaper; with it undelivered there is NO TES.
explanation.definitionFit: Notes are short, hastily written messages or memos.

clue.text: Encountered turbulent start of Russian nation

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so take the opening letter of Russian
turbulent means in disorder, so the letters of nation are shaken up

explanation.surface: A historical sketch of how a troubled Russian state began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of' takes R from Russian; 'turbulent' rearranges NATION to ANINTO.
explanation.definitionFit: To run into someone is an idiom for meeting them by chance.

clue.text: Corrupt document finally isn't

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word document

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: Someone insists a document is not corrupt after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes T, the last letter of document.
explanation.definitionFit: To taint something is to spoil or contaminate it, the same as to corrupt it.

clue.text: Shakespeare's to be second person, first could be Francis Bacon

parts.note: in Shakespeare's English 'thou art' is the second person singular of the verb to be
1st is written with the ordinal ending IST when the numeral is read as I

explanation.surface: A nod to the old theory that Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites the Shakespeare authorship debate, but the definition points to the twentieth-century painter Francis Bacon, not the Elizabethan philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon (1909-1992) was a celebrated painter, so he is an example of a painter or creator.

clue.text: River mammals in river, snakes in the grass

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps
otters are aquatic mammals living along rivers

explanation.surface: A riverbank scene with mammals swimming and snakes hidden in the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene suggests real animals, but 'snakes in the grass' is the idiom for treacherous people.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotters and snakes in the grass are both nasty, untrustworthy people, a matching insult.

clue.text: Gut instinct's three-quarters about outwardly tangible energy

indicators.note: about means going around, so the first piece wraps the second
three-quarters of the word keeps its first six of eight letters, dropping the end
outwardly means only the outside letters of tangible are kept

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A gut instinct mostly concerns energy that can be felt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three-quarters' cuts INSTINCT to INSTIN; 'outwardly' gives TE from tangible, which INSTIN goes 'about' to make INTESTIN, then E for energy.
explanation.definitionFit: The gut is the everyday name for the intestine, the bowel.

clue.text: The least roofless car in the competition

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a test is a contest, as in a Test match

indicators.note: roofless means the top letter is removed, as Mini is taken without its first letter

parts.note: the Mini is a classic small British car

explanation.surface: A convertible described as the smallest car in a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roofless' takes M off MINI to leave INI, which goes 'in' TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiniest is the smallest, the least in size.

clue.text: Sanctions designed to exclude foremost of caber tossers

indicators.note: designed suggests the letters of sanctions are rearranged, with one letter shut out of the result
foremost picks the first letter of caber

explanation.surface: Highland Games rules barring the leading caber tossers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed to exclude' rearranges SANCTIONS less C, the first letter of caber picked by 'foremost of'. 'tossers' looks like part of the caber phrase but is the definition, in its vulgar sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Onanists are masturbators, which is the literal British slang sense of tossers.

clue.text: Objective and popular speaker's pulling power

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: a speaker's version is how the word is said, not how it is written

parts.note: tension is the pulling force in a rope or cable

explanation.surface: A popular orator's aim and magnetic charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speaker's' signals that TENSION is only heard as -TENTION.
explanation.definitionFit: An intention is an aim or goal, which is what an objective is.

clue.text: Giant bird with origins in Arabian Nights

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: origins means the first letters of Arabian and Nights

explanation.surface: The giant roc bird of the Arabian Nights tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'origins in' takes A and N.
explanation.definitionFit: A titan is a person or thing of huge size, after the mythological race of giants.

clue.text: Quit wasting good dope!

indicators.note: wasting means losing, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: to resign is to quit a job

explanation.surface: An exasperated plea to a stoner not to waste good drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasting' takes G from RESIGN.
explanation.definitionFit: Cannabis resin is a common form of dope, slang for the drug.

clue.text: News coming in supports witness for the state

indicators.note: coming in means one piece goes inside another

parts.note: tees are the pegs supporting a golf ball
N is new, so news, two of them, is NN
to witness is to see

explanation.surface: A news report backing up a witness for the state prosecution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'News' looks like the media; it is read as N's, the plural of N for new. Golf tees are the supports, and 'coming in' puts the two Ns inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennessee is one of the fifty states of the USA.

clue.text: They make good soldiers among those on furlough

indicators.note: among puts one piece within the other

parts.note: people on furlough are resting, so they are resters
OR, other ranks, is the military abbreviation for ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers on leave being praised for behaving well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make good' looks like praise, but means repair.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good is to repair, so restorers are people who repair and renovate.

clue.text: The panel of 'Mock the Week'? Is it sprinkled with stars?

indicators.note: sprinkled suggests letters scattered about, so the letters are mixed together

explanation.surface: Asking whether a TV comedy panel show has celebrity guests.
explanation.walkthrough: Mock the Week was a British TV panel show of topical comedy. 'sprinkled with' mixes ISIT and STARS together.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedians on a topical show that mocks the news are satirists, people who ridicule current events.

clue.text: Stone circles one by one revealing Uralic language

indicators.note: circles means moves around, so the letters of stone change position

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
an means one, as in an apple

explanation.surface: Stone circles discovered one after another by archaeologists in Estonia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circles' rearranges STONE to ESTON, followed by I and AN for the two ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Estonian belongs to the Uralic family with Finnish and Hungarian, not to the Indo-European languages.

clue.text: Odd glimpses of station terminus from Fleet St

indicators.note: the odd glimpses are the odd-placed letters of station
a terminus is an end point, so the last letter of Fleet

explanation.surface: Glimpsing a station terminus from London's Fleet Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet St' reads as London's Fleet Street; the St actually stands for the answer. 'Odd glimpses of' gives SAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: St is the abbreviation for saint, as in St Paul.

clue.text: It is absent from 7 disease record

indicators.note: absent from means these letters go missing from the disease named

parts.note: 7 is INTESTINE, and enteritis is inflammation of the intestine

explanation.surface: A health record shows no sign of a gut illness.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' is the answer at 7-down, the gut, whose inflammation is ENTERITIS; 'It is' absent from that leaves ENTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter details is to record them, as in a register or ledger.

clue.text: Great for Brunel as each ship's back

parts.note: the stern is the rear of a ship

explanation.surface: Engineer Brunel praising every ship's rear section.
explanation.walkthrough: Isambard Kingdom Brunel's huge steamship was the Great Eastern, so this word follows Great in his ship's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunel's giant Victorian steamship was named the Great Eastern, so the answer completes that name.

clue.text: European IT errors holding up our pupils' targets?

indicators.note: in a down entry up means the letters are read from bottom to top
the words European IT errors hold the answer within them

explanation.surface: European computer errors delaying schoolchildren's exam targets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' hides EANITER across European IT errors; 'up' turns it round. The pupils are those of the eyes, not school pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: Light passing through the pupil of the eye lands on the retina, so the retinae are what pupils aim at.

clue.text: Savour speed, making Hamilton's start time

indicators.note: making here means turning one letter into another

parts.note: hastiness is haste, speed

indicators.note: start points to the first letter of Hamilton's

explanation.surface: Lewis Hamilton, the Formula One driver, savouring his speed and a fast start time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making ... time' swaps the H that starts Hamilton's in HASTINESS for T.
explanation.definitionFit: Savour as a noun is flavour, the quality of being tasty or delicious.

clue.text: Without hesitating spinster stripped naked in front of six-footer

indicators.note: in front of places the first piece before the second
stripped naked means all outer layers are removed, here two letters from each end of spinster

parts.note: an ant is an insect, with six legs or feet

explanation.surface: A spinster rushing to undress in front of a very tall man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped naked' removes SP and ER, the two outer layers each side, leaving INST. 'six-footer' suggests a tall person but is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Something instant happens immediately, with no delay or hesitation.

clue.text: Japanese teacher said "Time I'm going" with feeling

indicators.note: said means the teacher's title is taken as it is pronounced, SEN-SAY

parts.note: a sensei is a Japanese teacher or martial arts master

indicators.note: going means these letters leave

parts.note: taken as the full word time
taken as the letters of I'm without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A martial arts master feelingly announcing that it is time to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: SENSEI is spoken SEN-SAY, written SENSA; 'going' takes I'M from TIME to leave TE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensate means perceiving through the senses, so endowed with feeling or sensation.

clue.text: It could improve your mood to snore in turns

indicators.note: turns means the letters are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Sharing the snoring at night might cheer up a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' mixes TO and SNORE together, with IN left as it stands at the end; 'in turns' looks like one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Serotonin is a brain chemical linked to well-being; low levels are associated with depression.

clue.text: Unsportsmanlike yo-yoing?

definitions.meaning: British slang for unacceptable or unfair conduct

explanation.surface: Is it bad sportsmanship to play with a yo-yo?
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: like a yo-yo going down and back up, the answer reads the same in either direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Not on is British slang for unacceptable, so conduct that is unfair or unsporting.

clue.text: Armchairs should be this material

explanation.definitionFit: Satin is a glossy fabric, and an armchair exists to be sat in, splitting the word.

clue.text: Meal including fillets of tender fish

indicators.note: including means the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: tea is an evening meal in British usage

indicators.note: fillets suggest the edges trimmed away, keeping the first and last letters of tender

explanation.surface: A dinner of tender fish fillets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fillets of' gives TR, which TEA is 'including'. Tea in Britain is often the evening meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetra is a small tropical freshwater fish popular in aquariums.

clue.text: Tin symbolically represented German industrial centre

indicators.note: represented means the two letters are written out as their spoken names

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin

explanation.surface: Tin as the symbol of a German manufacturing city.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters S and N, spelled out as words, are ESS and EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is a city in the Ruhr, Germany's historic coal and steel region.

clue.text: Flower against Vauxhall bridges

indicators.note: bridges means spans over, so one piece is placed across the other

parts.note: the Astra is a model of car made by Vauxhall
anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: A floral display against a London bridge at Vauxhall.
explanation.walkthrough: Vauxhall is a London district with a Thames bridge, but here it is the British car maker, whose Astra is a family hatchback.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrantia, or masterwort, is a garden plant with star-shaped blooms.

clue.text: Former statesman and astronaut's body's pronounced sound

indicators.note: pronounced sound means the word's sound when spoken aloud is what counts

parts.note: NASA is the US space agency, the body employing astronauts, so NASA's

explanation.surface: A politician and a space traveller with a loud voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' looks like an astronaut's physique; it is an organisation, NASA.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamal Abdel Nasser was president of Egypt from 1956 until 1970.

clue.text: Parasite going into eyes via the ear feasted on blood

indicators.note: going into means one piece is inserted in another
via the ear means the word is taken as it sounds

parts.note: the word eyes, heard, is two letters I
a nit is a head louse egg, a parasite
to have feasted is to have eaten, ate

explanation.surface: A blood-sucking parasite getting into the eyes and feeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eyes' heard is I's, so II, which NIT is 'going into'. 'blood' looks like a noun; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To blood a newcomer is to give a first experience of something, which is to initiate them.
